analysis.one_liner: Negotiates Medicare prices on far more drugs and lets negotiation start years sooner after launch.
analysis.headline: The bill has been stuck in the Senate Finance Committee since it was referred there on introduction, with 26 senators signed on and no committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthens the Medicare drug price negotiation program created by the Inflation Reduction Act. It raises the number of drugs selected for negotiation each year from 15 to 50, cuts from 7 and 11 years to 3 years the period after a drug's launch during which it is shielded from selection, and steepens the maximum prices Medicare can pay — for example, lowering the ceiling for newer drugs from 65% to 55% of their list price. It would apply to prices starting in 2028. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, whose out-of-pocket and premium costs track the prices Medicare pays, plus taxpayers, who help fund Medicare drug spending. If more drugs face lower negotiated prices sooner after launch, savings reach seniors years earlier than under current law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the number of drugs Medicare selects for price negotiation each year from 15 to 50 and removes the scheduled future limits, covering far more of seniors' drug spending. [S2]

It cuts the post-launch shield from negotiation from 7 years for most drugs and 11 years for biologics down to 3 years, so prices can be negotiated while the drug is still on the market rather than near the end of its exclusivity. [S2]

It steepens the maximum fair price ceilings Medicare can negotiate — lowering them from 65% to 55% and from 40% to 30% of a drug's list price for newer drugs — which pushes negotiated prices down further. [S2]
The changes apply to negotiated prices beginning with the 2028 applicability year. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biotech manufacturers, who would face negotiation on far more products, years earlier in each drug's life, at deeper discounts. To the extent savings flow through Medicare, the federal budget gains and taxpayers shoulder less; drugmakers argue earlier and deeper negotiation reduces revenue available to reinvest in developing new medicines.

drawbacks.text: Earlier and deeper negotiation reduces revenue for pharmaceutical manufacturers; the industry's good-faith argument is that this money funds research and development, and that cutting it early in a drug's life could shrink investment in some medicines. [S2]

The bill changes only the Medicare negotiation program; it does nothing about drug prices for the roughly half of Americans with private insurance or no insurance, so its benefit is limited to the Medicare population. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers the gains are direct and large: more drugs negotiated sooner, at lower ceilings, starting in 2028. The real trade-off is the uncertain effect on future drug innovation, which is a genuine but unquantified cost, and the fact that the bill leaves drug prices for non-Medicare patients untouched. On balance the design is a straightforward tightening of an existing program rather than a restructuring, so the downside risks are narrower than the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day and has had no committee vote or floor action since, while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the SMART Prices Act on May 21, 2025, with 26 senators signed on — 25 of the 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 Independents — and no Republicans. [S2] [S3] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over Medicare, and no further action has been recorded. [S4]

The bill amends the Medicare drug price negotiation program created by the Inflation Reduction Act: 50 drugs selected per year, a 3-year post-launch shield instead of 7 or 11 years, and lower price ceilings, effective for prices starting in 2028. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off so far: with the bill sitting in committee, the deeper Medicare negotiation it would impose has not moved. Seniors and taxpayers have gained nothing yet either.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 26 of 47 Senate Democrats and Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on the day of introduction — no hearing, no markup, no vote recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents (25 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Independents); no Republican cosponsor has joined, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill expands and accelerates Medicare price negotiation and deepens the discounts Medicare can demand, cutting directly into brand-name drug revenue. Savings flow to seniors' drug costs and the Medicare program rather than to the companies.
Lower negotiated Medicare prices reduce premiums and cost-sharing for seniors and reduce federal drug spending funded by taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, the bill is following the usual path of Medicare drug-pricing bills in a divided Senate: it will likely remain in the Finance Committee unless drug pricing becomes a priority in a must-pass vehicle like a broader health or funding package.
